title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and our ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers designing services or making changes that impact production reliability, cost, or developer ergonomics.

Sections and intent
- API standards: consistent REST/JSON semantics, versioning, auth, error handling and pagination patterns for the Redwood API and internal services.
- Coding standards: language-specific conventions and code hygiene expectations for service owners.
- Infra standards: IaC, network topology, secrets management, and deployment patterns for cloud and private deployments.
- Model-serving standards: runtime expectations, model packaging, quantization profiles, KV cache and batching configurations.
- Observability standards: metrics, tracing, logging, dashboards and alerting thresholds.
- Performance standards: SLOs, benchmarks, test harnesses, and perf testing practices.
- ADRs: how to record architectural decisions and link them to projects and rollouts.

API Standards (applies to internal and public endpoints)
1) API design principles - Use resource-oriented endpoints (nouns not verbs). Prefer POST for complex operations that produce resources (e.g., /v1/streams, /v1/generate) and GET for idempotent retrieval.
- APIs are JSON-over-HTTPS only. All endpoints must serve application/json and use UTF-8.
- Keep request/response schemas explicit and documented in OpenAPI 3.1. Maintain the OpenAPI spec in the repo alongside implementation.

2) Versioning - Path-based major versioning: /v1/... for public APIs. Semantic versioning for extension-quality changes is reflected in the OpenAPI spec and release notes.
- Backwards-compatible additions (optional fields) do not require a new major version. Breaking changes require a documented migration plan and at least 30 days of deprecation notice.

3) Auth and RBAC - Primary auth for APIs is bearer tokens (short-lived API keys for services; long-lived developer keys are allowed behind UI controls).
- All internal service-to-service calls must use mTLS (where supported) or signed tokens issued by the identity service.
- Sensitive endpoints (model-management, billing, audit) must enforce RBAC scopes with least privilege.

4) Error handling and status codes - Use standard HTTP status codes. Return a JSON error envelope with fields: code (string), message (string), request_id (string), and details (optional string). Example: {"code":"MODEL_NOT_FOUND","message":"Model 'redwood-alpha' not found","request_id":"..."}.
- Error codes are short UPPER_SNAKE strings, documented in the API spec. Client retries should rely on status codes and Retry-After header when present.

5) Pagination and streaming - For list endpoints use cursor-based pagination: {"items":[], "next_cursor":"..."}. Avoid offset pagination at scale.
- Long-running or streaming responses should use chunked transfer (server-sent events / streaming HTTP) or WebSockets as appropriate. Streams must include a canonical final event with status.

6) Rate limiting and idempotency - All public endpoints include rate limiting; service owners must declare the target QPS and burst behavior.
- Endpoints that create resources must support idempotency via Idempotency-Key header. Duplicate operations must be safe within a 24-hour window unless otherwise documented.

Coding Standards
- Languages and formatting - Use the official style guides for languages in use: Go (gofmt, golangci-lint), Python (Black, flake8, mypy), TypeScript (Prettier, ESLint, strict mode).
- Small PRs, descriptive titles, and single-concern changes. Maximum PR size guideline: < 400 lines changed for application code; for infra changes coordinate with owners.

- Testing - Unit tests for all public functions and business logic. Target 80% coverage for critical libraries; services should include integration tests for major workflows.
- Contract tests: services exposing an API must include contract tests that run against mock/staging deployments and fail CI if broken.

- Dependency management - Use pinned versions and Dependabot-style automated updates with required PR reviews. For native libs affecting inference runtime (C/C++ kernels), require a perf/regression guard rail before upgrade.

Infra Standards
- IaC and provisioning - All infrastructure must be managed via Terraform modules stored in the terraform repo. Modules must define explicit input/output variables and use versioned releases (git tags).
- Environment parity: dev -> staging -> prod must use the same modules with different variable sets. No manual changes allowed in prod (changes are authorized via PR + CI).

- Networking and VPC - Services must be deployed to segmented VPCs with least-privilege security groups. Public-facing endpoints sit behind API gateway and WAF. Private deployments (customer VPCs) must follow the reference architecture in /confluence/eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures.

- Secrets & keys - Use KMS-backed secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault depending on environment). Secrets must never be checked into git. Rotate keys on schedule: service tokens every 90 days; long-lived infra keys every 365 days with automated rotation tooling.

- CI/CD and deployment patterns - Blue/green or canary-by-traffic rollout is required for any change that affects inference runtime behavior. CI must run unit + integration + contract + perf smoke tests prior to rollout.

Model-Serving Standards
- Model packaging and metadata - Models must be packaged with a manifest JSON including: model_id, architecture (e.g., LLaMA2-70B), precision profile (fp16/int8/q4_0), tokenization config, KV-cache-enabled (true/false), and quantization profile id. Store model manifests in the model-registry service.

- Quantization and performance profiles - Define quantization profiles in /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles. Each profile should include expected throughput, memory footprint, and recommended hardware class (A100, H100, T4, etc.). Changes to quantization must be accompanied by accuracy regression tests.

- Batching and latency tradeoffs - Default batching policy: target batch size should be adaptive based on observed request latency and model characteristics. Service owners must provide a latency SLO (e.g., P95 < 150 ms for short-context generates). Use continuous batching where feasible; ensure cold-start latency remains within SLO.

- KV cache and prefix caching - Token-level KV cache should be exposed as a configurable option with TTL and size limits. Cache keys must include model_id + model_digest + cache_config. Provide metrics for cache hit rate and eviction count.

- Model versioning and rollouts - Support pinned model versions and automatic fallback to compatible variants. Rollouts must include canary traffic (default 5% -> 25% -> 100%) and automated acceptance checks (latency, error rate, quality metrics on canary prompts).

- Safety and guardrails - Model-serving endpoints must integrate with safety filters (input sanitization and post-response filters) and maintain audit logs for requests when in restricted deployments.

Observability Standards
- Metrics - Follow the service naming convention: redwood.<service>.<component>.<metric>. Metrics must include: request_count (counter), request_latencies_ms (histogram), error_count (counter by error_code), batch_size (histogram). Export metrics in Prometheus format.

- Tracing - Use OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing. Trace ids must be propagated across service boundaries. Instrument critical spans: auth, routing, model-exec, cache-lookup, batching. Target span durations to align with service SLOs.

- Logging - Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, service, component, request_id, trace_id, msg, metadata. Avoid logging PII or customer secrets. Logs should be sampled if high volume, with full sampling on errors.

- Dashboards and alerting
- Standard dashboards per service: Overview (traffic, latency P95/P99, error rate), Batching & Throughput, Model Execution (GPU utilization), Cache stats.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - page if error_rate (5m) > 1% AND request_count (5m) > 1000
  - page if P99 latency (5m) > 2x SLO AND request_count (5m) > 500
  - page on sustained GPU memory pressure > 90% for 10m

Performance Standards
- SLOs and SLIs - Default SLO for public inference: P95 latency <= 250ms for short-context (<=128 tokens) and error_rate <= 0.5%. Dedicated deployments may have tighter SLOs per contract. Service owners must declare SLOs in the service's SLO doc and register them with the SLO system.

- Benchmarking and perf tests - Use the benchmarking harness in /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. Benchmarks must include representative prompt sets, sequence-length distributions, and concurrency profiles. Command-line example: 
  ./perf-runner --model redwood-small --concurrency 32 --seq 128 --profile full_prompt_set.yaml

- Regression testing and release gates - Any change to runtime kernels, quantization, or model packaging requires running the perf suite and the eval harness with a regression acceptance criteria file. Releases that degrade P95 by > 10% or increase mean cost/token by > 8% must be blocked until mitigations are implemented.

ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
- Purpose and format - Record significant architecture decisions in ADRs stored in the architecture repo and referenced from confluence. Each ADR should contain: ADR ID (e.g., ADR-2026-03), status (proposed|accepted|deprecated), context, decision, consequences, and owners.

- Lifecycle - Proposed ADRs are discussed in design reviews. After approval, ADRs are marked accepted and linked in the relevant service docs and release notes. Deprecated ADRs must include migration steps.

- Example ADRs (summary)
  - ADR-2025-12: Default model packaging format (manifest + artifacts tarball)
  - ADR-2026-01: Standardizing on OpenTelemetry for tracing across services
  - ADR-2026-02: Canary rollout policy and automated rollback thresholds

Standards Compliance and Review Process
- Service owners are responsible for compliance. New services must complete the Architecture Checklist:
  1) API spec in OpenAPI in repo
  2) SLO doc registered
  3) Terraform modules used for infra
  4) CI gates for unit/integration/contract/perf
  5) Observability dashboards created
- Quarterly architecture reviews will audit a sampling of services for standards compliance. Non-compliant services will be assigned remediation owners and tracked until closed.

Appendices
A. Minimal API error envelope (JSON){"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"Unexpected error","request_id":"req_123","details":"optional detail for debugging"}

B. Standard metric names (examples)
- redwood.api.requests_total
- redwood.api.request_duration_seconds_bucket
- redwood.model.exec_latency_ms
- redwood.model.kv_cache_hit_ratio

C. Canary rollout checklist (operational)
1) Create canary release and target 5% traffic for 10 minutes.
2) Run canary acceptance tests: latency, errors, sample prompt quality checks.
3) If thresholds unchanged, move to 25% for 30 minutes.
4) If stable, expand to 100% and mark release complete.
5) If any step fails automated checks, rollback and open incident review.

D. ADR template (file header)
- ADR ID:
- Title:
- Status: proposed|accepted|deprecated
- Date:
- Author:
- Context:
- Decision:
- Consequences:
- Related ADRs:
